Explain how multi-head self-attention works to a systems engineer with linear algebra background in 3 crisp paragraphs.
text_before.content:
Multi-head self-attention starts with a sequence of token embeddings \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\), where \(n\) is sequence length and \(d\) is model dimension. For each head, \(X\) is linearly projected into query, key, and value matrices: \(Q = XW_Q\), \(K = XW_K\), \(V = XW_V\). The attention scores are computed as \(A = \text{softmax}(QK^\top / \sqrt{d_k})\), where \(QK^\top\) measures similarity between every token pair, and the softmax normalizes each row into a probability distribution over tokens.

The output of one head is \(A V\), a weighted sum of value vectors where each token aggregates information from all other tokens according to learned relevance. Multi-head attention runs this operation in parallel across \(h\) heads, each with its own projection matrices, producing \(h\) outputs \(H_i = A_i V_i\). These are concatenated and projected back to the model dimension: \(\text{MHA}(X) = \text{Concat}(H_1,\dots,H_h)W_O\).

From a systems perspective, multi-head self-attention is a parallel, data-dependent routing mechanism: each head learns a different similarity metric and information pathway, allowing the model to attend to syntax, semantics, positional patterns, and other relationships simultaneously. The cost is dominated by the \(n \times n\) attention matrix, so it is compute- and memory-intensive for long sequences, which is why optimized kernels, batching, and sparse/approximate attention variants matter in production systems.
